appraisal_events.evidence: « Jeunes et tendres fleurs par le sort agitées, / Sous un ciel étranger comme moi transplantées / Dans un lieu séparé de profanes témoins, / Il (l’excellent ambassadeur) met à les former son étude et ses soins. »
appraisal_events.explanation: The passage continues the Racinian Esther speech that the narrator has lent to the silent, staring M. de Vaugoubert, and the interpolated gloss "(l'excellent ambassadeur)" converts the pious lines about Mardochée's chosen maidens into a deadpan innuendo about an embassy stocked with hand-picked young secretaries. The mock-classical ventriloquism diminishes Vaugoubert by exposing the concupiscent reading his gaze is performing, while the sardonic epithet "excellent" simultaneously deflates the ambassador it names.

status_effects.explanation: Vaugoubert is locally lowered: he is given no words of his own, and the classical verses the narrator supplies for him make his mute ogling legible and faintly ridiculous.

ambiguities: "l'excellent ambassadeur" is a narrator's gloss on the Esther verses and does not denote Norpois, despite "l'Ambassadeur" being a registered alias for him: the immediately preceding sentence identifies the referent as the unnamed "ambassadeur de X… en France, vieux cheval de retour", who is an off-sheet unnamed figure and so is not listed among characters_present even though the sardonic epithet targets him directly.

This unit is a bare continuation of a quotation begun in the previous unit, so whether the ironic force falls chiefly on M. de Vaugoubert (the mute gazer for whom the narrator recites the lines) or on the ambassador named in the parenthesis depends on framing that lies just outside the unit; Vaugoubert is taken as the target because the whole classical graft is staged as the speech of his eyes.
